title: Shepherds who feed themselves (Ezekiel 34)
hookLine: leaders who fleece the flock; God will seek the lost and bind the broken

cards: Ezekiel has been speaking to exiles who have lost almost everything: their land, their Temple, their king. Today he turns from the people to the people in charge.

In his chapter, the leaders of Israel are called shepherds, an old picture for anyone whose job is to feed and keep a flock. And he has a question for them, the kind that stings because the answer is obvious.

teach.h: SHOULD NOT THE SHEPHERDS FEED THE FLOCK?
teach.b: The question is blunt. In the King James words: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?" Then the charges, one by one.
You eat the fat and wear the wool. You kill the well-fed ones. But the weak you have not strengthened.
The sick you have not healed. The broken you have not bound up. The ones driven away you have not brought back.
The lost you have not looked for. Instead, you ruled them with force and with harshness. So the sheep scattered, became food for wild animals, and no one went looking for them.
It isn't a list of grand crimes. It's neglect: a leader who takes what the job gives and skips what the job asks. Then the chapter turns, and God says, in effect: then I will do it myself.

teach.h: THE WEAK, THE SICK, THE BROKEN, THE LOST.
teach.b: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick."

Almost every failure on the first list is answered by a promise on the second. The text even judges between sheep and sheep: the strong ones who push with shoulder and horn and muddy the water the others have to drink.

teach.h: I WILL SEEK THAT WHICH WAS LOST.
teach.b: The Bible says that Moses and David both kept sheep before they led anyone.

A midrash tells that Moses was chosen after he followed one runaway young goat to a pool of water and carried it back on his shoulders. The leader in this chapter goes looking for the one who wandered off.

how: Jews read Ezekiel 34 among the Latter Prophets, and the image of the leader as shepherd is taught through the stories of Moses and David caring for their flocks.

o: priests, who offer sacrifices at the Temple
kings' soldiers, who guard the city gates
leaders, who should feed and care for their flock

games.q: shepherds who feed themselves — tap the pairs.
p: carried back by Moses in a midrash

s: Ezekiel's charge is mostly about neglect
the weak, the sick, the broken, the driven away and the lost were left uncared for.
the chapter ends with the sheep left scattered
God promises to seek the lost and bind up the broken.
the chapter only judges the shepherds
it also judges between sheep and sheep, the strong who push the weak aside.

games.q: the shepherds have fed themselves and let the flock scatter. what does the chapter say happens next?
o: the flock is left to fend for itself.
new shepherds are hired from abroad.
God says: I will seek the lost myself.
games.why: God takes up the work the shepherds skipped: seek the lost, bring back the driven away, bind up the broken, strengthen the sick.

practice: Think of a flock that's yours already: a kid, a team, a younger sibling, an aging parent, a friend who leans on you.

Go down Ezekiel's list slowly, who's weak, who's sick, who's been hurt, who has drifted away, and let one face come. Just hold that person, the way a shepherd might carry a stray back; if you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: shepherds, the leaders Ezekiel accuses of feeding themselves while the flock goes hungry, sick, and lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: shepherd, the word Ezekiel uses for the leaders of Israel.

carryVoice: Your line: seek the lost. Ezekiel's second list answers the first. That's day eight hundred twelve.
